frames.narration: A technician is in a basement with no signal. She marks work order WO-17 as done and records that she used 3 parts. The app writes both changes to the local database and adds two outbox rows, d1-41 and d1-42, in one local transaction. The screen updates at once.
Meanwhile the manager, who is online, raises the priority of WO-17 on a tablet. The server merges it and gives it sequence number 18,205 in the change log.
Forty minutes later the technician climbs out and the signal returns. The sync loop sends the two pending mutations in one batch, each with its id.

The two edits touch different fields from the manager's priority, so nothing conflicts. Status is set to done by the technician and priority stays high from the manager. The parts count is stored as a change of minus 3, so it adds to any other change instead of replacing it. The log records sequence numbers 18,206 and 18,207.

The reply is lost in a tunnel, so the app does not know the batch arrived and sends it again. The server recognises d1-41 and d1-42 and acknowledges them without applying anything, so the parts count is still minus 3 and not minus 6.

Now the app pulls. It asks for work order changes after its cursor, 18,200. The log holds 7 changes the technician may see, 18,201 to 18,207, including the manager's priority. The app applies them and saves the new cursor, 18,207, in one transaction.
The tablet gets a push hint, pulls, and shows WO-17 as done with 3 parts used. Two devices that never talked to each other now hold identical data.

Another technician switches on a phone that was in a drawer for 45 days. Its cursor, 9,100, is below the server's floor, because tombstones older than 35 days have been collected. The server answers with a reset, and the app downloads a fresh snapshot of about 0.6 MB, which also drops the rows that were deleted while it was away.
